item.title: Ole Miss and LSU will deliver cinema, but the next week for each team could be their most pivotal tests
item.description: Lane Kiffin returns to Oxford as LSU's coach to face Ole Miss and former players Trinidad Chambliss and Kewan Lacy in a Top 10 SEC showdown.
item.content:encoded:
The most-anticipated game of the college football regular season will take place in Oxford, Miss., on Saturday night, with a gold-and-purple-clad Lane Kiffin returning to town to take on the team and fanbase he abandoned just 10 months ago.

On paper, the LSU-Ole Miss matchup features everything a college football game could ever want. For starters, it's a historic rivalry matchup featuring two Top 10 teams with huge SEC Championship and College Football Playoff implications on the line. You add in the Kiffin of it all, and the contest goes from just a great college football game to a full-blown spectacle.

If Kiffin's first game against Ole Miss as the head coach at LSU were being held in Baton Rouge, it wouldn't have nearly as much of a mystique around it. Thankfully, the football gods had it made that this game would be played in Mississippi.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

If you're an LSU fan, there has to be something at least slightly unsettling about Kiffin and his $50 million Tigers roster coming to Oxford to take on an Ole Miss team headlined by quarterback Trinidad Chambliss and running back Kewan Lacy, two players Kiffin and his staff fought to come join them on the bayou. Leaving Oxford without a win would deliver a dose of reality to both Tigers fans and Kiffin himself that perhaps things aren't quite as they seem, at least not yet.

On the other sideline, you have an Ole Miss team that not only lost key pieces from last season, but is also being coached by a man in Pete Golding, who is entering just his sixth game as a head coach. You also have a fanbase foaming at the mouth to see Kiffin squirm on the opposing sideline inside the stadium he coached in for six seasons.

In terms of question marks, Ole Miss has the most between the two teams heading into Saturday, but they could also have the answers in the form of Chambliss and Lacy, two Heisman Trophy candidates.

The angles of what makes Saturday's game simply so massive are virtually endless, and while the game itself will undoubtedly deliver, the contests that both teams will have to play in just seven days later could very well be the most pivotal ones of their respective seasons.

Ole Miss travels to Gainesville to take on Florida in Week 4, and if the Gators take care of Auburn on the road this Saturday, The Swamp will be absolutely jumping when the Rebels arrive. That statement will be true whether Ole Miss beats LSU or loses by three touchdowns. Florida head coach Jon Sumrall will be looking to catch an Ole Miss team at the right time, with the Rebels coming off an unbelievably emotional week.

LSU has the luxury of returning home to Death Valley in Week 4, but has to welcome Texas A&M to town. The Aggies play Kentucky at home in Week 3, meaning they'll likely arrive in Baton Rouge unbeaten and as a Top 10 program in the nation. Many would argue that Texas A&M is the most overlooked team of the young college football season up to this point, but taking down LSU in Baton Rouge would certainly flip that narrative.

In a world where college football chatter has become more focused on court cases and NIL money, it's these sets of factors and matchups that still make the sport so great. The SEC adding an additional conference game to the slate this season is also being felt in this particular scenario, and it's going to be fascinating to see how teams respond to an extra, very stiff test.

Nothing would be more college football than seeing the winner of the Ole Miss-LSU throwdown turn around and lose just seven days later. Whatever happens, we'll all be watching.

item.title: ‘Trojan horses’ in America: Congress probes influence networks tied to China, Iran and Cuba
item.description: Lawmakers will examine alleged foreign malign influence operations tied to China, Iran and Cuba after Fox News Digital traced pro-communist network operating inside the U.S.
item.content:encoded:
Last Tuesday, at the corner of Church Street and 16th Street NW, blocks from the White House, Christine Balling, a former advisor to U.S. Special Operations Command South, led a panel discussion on the national security threat that communist-run Cuba poses to the U.S.

Suddenly, a fresh-faced former college basketball star, Olivia DiNucci, stood up to steal the stage at the Institute of World Politics, yelling as she clutched a hand-painted banner: "SANCTIONS KILL IN CUBA."

"There is global solidarity with Gaza and Cuba and ICE here," DiNucci shouted breathlessly, as security officials grabbed her banner and pushed her out a side door as she kept yelling, "because the liberation of our people is rooted in our neighbors!"

In small print, the banner had DiNucci's organizational and ideological affiliation: "CODEPINK."

DiNucci is a D.C.-based political organizer with CodePink, a left-wing political agitation group, spending her days and evenings as a professional protester and a regular gadfly, disrupting dinners, hearings and conferences as a sidekick to CodePink co-founder Susan Medea Benjamin. Their group supports the Communist Party of Cuba and has led caravans to the island nation, as Treasury Department officials investigate whether they violated any laws barring Americans from doing business with the communist regime.

For Balling and her co-panelist, Michael Gonzalez, a senior fellow at the Heritage Foundation and a Cuban American firmly opposed to the communist government of Cuba, DiNucci's political theater wasn't the benign act of an "anti-war" group, as CodePink describes itself.

"CodePink – and other organizations like it – essentially act like Trojan horses. They burst in onto the scene, and they're meant to disrupt and destroy from within," Balling told Fox News Digital.

"They're really interested in dividing America and, in doing so, weakening it," she continued, "and increasing the friction between Americans by convincing some Americans that the American idea, the American dream, the freedoms we enjoy, all that sort of thing, that they are lies and they're not worth fighting for, and that our enemies are our victims."

POWER COUPLE OF CHAOS: HOW A TYCOON AND ACTIVIST BUILT A 'REVOLUTIONARY BASE' AT THE HOUSE OF SINGHAM

The confrontation comes as House lawmakers convene a hearing on Tuesday, titled "Trojan Horses: Covert Foreign Malign Influence Operations in America," to examine a broad question: how do American activists, nonprofit organizations, media operations and social media influencers, like Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, advance the interests of adversarial nations, including China, Iran and Cuba, inside the United States?

Piker joined CodePink's delegation to Cuba earlier this year, posing for a photo in Havana with CodePink cofounder, Jodie Evans, both of them also drawing Treasury Department scrutiny.

"Adversarial nations like China, Russia, and Cuba conduct malign influence operations here in the United States by utilizing social media influencers such as Hasan Piker as proxies to promote communism and push their false propaganda," Rep. Bill Huizenga, R-Mich., chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on South and Central Asia, told Fox News Digital.

"My goal is to raise the curtain to expose these operations and stop them from undermining our national security, capitalism and the American Dream," Huizenga said.

HASAN PIKER CALLS HAMAS 'FAR MORE MODERATE,' DISMISSES TERROR GROUP’S BRUTAL RULE IN GAZA

The hearing will bring together several strands of alleged foreign influence that Fox News Digital has documented over the past year through investigations into money, political organizing, overseas travel, media operations and relationships between American activists and foreign entities and interests. Most of the groups fall into the "red-green alliance" of socialist and communist groups, symbolized by the color red, working closely with Islamist groups, such as the anti-Israel organization Students for Justice in Palestine, reflected by the color green, a symbol of Islam.

The largest financial network examined in Fox News Digital's reporting centers on Neville Roy Singham, an American-born tech tycoon who lives in Shanghai, late last year standing on a stage at the Golden Tulip Hotel during a conference on the "Global South," delivering a speech supporting the Chinese Communist Party, China's leader, Xi Jinping and China's "new world order."

RUBIO'S CALL TO COMBAT GLOBAL FUNDERS OF FAR-LEFT TERRORISM COULD PUT SINGHAM IN CROSSHAIRS

A five-part Fox News Digital investigation published earlier this year examined 223 transactions totaling $591 million across five continents between 2017 and 2025, tracing the flow of money through multiple layers of organizations and into a transnational network estimated at approximately 2,000 organizations.

In 2017, Singham married Evans, the CodePink co-founder, in a ceremony in Jamaica attended by Benjamin and other pro-communist leaders. The Fox News Digital analysis documented $278 million flowing from Singham into six core nonprofit organizations that promulgate anti-America, pro-China propaganda, beginning in 2017: BreakThrough BT Media Inc., CodePink Women for Peace, Justice and Education Fund Inc., People's Forum Inc., People's Support Foundation Ltd. and Tricontinental Ltd.

The organizations and their executives have denied any wrongdoing and allege they are the target of anti-communist "witch hunts." Singham hasn't responded to repeated requests for comment.

CUBA BUILT COVERT NETWORK INSIDE AMERICA THROUGH SPIES, ACTIVISTS AND UNIVERSITIES, STATE DEPT ALLEGES

Huizenga and the hearing's witnesses say Congress must examine whether adversarial governments are influencing American political discourse through domestic messengers while keeping the foreign power itself at arm's length.

Fox News Digital's reporting followed the money to the six nonprofits:

That was only the first layer. The six nonprofits that directly received Singham money subsequently distributed approximately $163 million to 52 organizations — including themselves — and five geographic regions identified in financial records.

Eleven groups at another layer distributed approximately $150 million into four nonprofits and five geographic regions, including $23 million directed to Sub-Saharan Africa, according to the Fox News Digital analysis.

The financial architecture has been accompanied by political organizing, media operations and ideological activity that includes the fresh example of political theater that CodePink unleashed at this week's disruption at the Institute of World Politics' panel on Cuba.

Balling, the former advisor to U.S. Special Operations Southern Command, used the opportunity to illustrate exactly the point that the Heritage Foundation's Gonzalez and she were arguing.

"Their method of operation," she said, "is to disrupt, of course, to get the soundbites on Twitter or Instagram or what have you, but they are not ever interested in a respectful dialogue."

"What was extraordinary is I was actually about to talk about CodePink and the Democratic Socialists of America, the DSA, as both being members of the largest pro-Cuban regime organization in the United States, called the National Network on Cuba," said Balling.

"And so the fact that she stood up and tried to disrupt the event was just a wonderful example for the audience," of the antics of CodePink. "They are actually really a mouthpiece for anti-American causes, which happen to be very pro-Chinese Communist Party causes and...the Castro regime."

On cue, at 6:42 p.m., less than an hour after the event had ended at about 6 p.m., CodePink posted a carefully curated and captioned 1-minute-35-second video of the DiNucci outburst on X. The same video went up on CodePink's official YouTube channel.

Balling said CodePink's messaging promoted "the interests of, frankly, our enemies, the Chinese Communist Party and then the Cuban regime."

"Their method of operation," she said, "is to disrupt, of course, to get the soundbites on Twitter or Instagram or what have you, but they are not ever interested in a respectful dialogue."

Sure enough, CodePink posted the video on its official Instagram account, tagging DiNucci.

"Frankly, had she been willing to stop screaming," said Balling, Gonzalez and she "would have actually been thrilled to have a debate with her, but that's not their way of operating."

By the end of the night, the disruption had also become a press release on CodePink's website, listing DiNucci herself as the "media contact" and offering journalists "unbranded video footage."

Fox News Digital's Jesse Watson and Brooke Curto contributed to this report.

item.title: House Dems face Trump tariff dilemma as major Russia sanctions bill heads to floor
item.description: The Lindsey Graham sanctions bill forces House Democrats to weigh Ukraine support against expanding Trump tariff authority they've long opposed.
item.content:encoded:
House Democrats will soon have to grapple with a decision over whether to give President Donald Trump more tariff authority or potentially block Congress from cracking down on Vladimir Putin's bloody war in Ukraine.

The House Rules Committee has teed up votes on several bills this week, including the Senate's legislation aimed at sanctioning Russia and Iran.

That bill was named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., a massive supporter of Ukraine who died unexpectedly at the age of 71 in July.

And while the majority of Democrats support action to help Ukraine against Russia's invasion, they'll also be forced to reckon with the legislation's language giving Trump additional authority to punish Russia and its allies with significant tariffs.

LINDSEY GRAHAM'S FINAL MISSION TO PUNISH PUTIN CLEARS SENATE AFTER YEARLONG FIGHT

Democrats have long been critical of Trump's unchecked use of tariffs against U.S. allies like Canada and Mexico, which have also been subject to a slew of court battles.

TRUMP JUST EXPANDED HIS TARIFF PLAYBOOK WITH A POWERFUL TRADE WEAPON NO PRESIDENT HAS EVER USED

It's part of why senior House Democrats said earlier this year that they would oppose the bill.

"House Democrats are rock solid in our support for Ukraine, but the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia And Iran Act would do more harm than good. This bill would dramatically expand presidential tariff authorities while failing to mandate sanctions on Russia, both of which are unacceptable," Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., Ranking Member of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, Rep. Richard Neal, D-Mass., Ranking Member of the House Committee on Ways and Means, and Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., said in a statement.

SEN RAND PAUL: DC'S RUSSIA SANCTIONS BILL WON'T STOP PUTIN — BUT IT WILL HURT YOU

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., did not give up his position on the bill during a Monday press conference, telling reporters, "We're going to continue to stand by the Ukrainian people and find a path forward to get a sanctions bill done while addressing the very real concerns that [Democrats] have raised about giving Donald Trump authority that the Supreme Court recently made clear he does not currently have, and should not have, because it belongs to the Congress pursuant to the Constitution."

The bill would direct the president to hike up to 500% tariffs on Russia and up to 100% on countries buying Russian energy.

MIKE PENCE: CONGRESS MUST FINISH LINDSEY GRAHAM’S FIGHT AGAINST PUTIN

Trump would also be directed to impose significant sanctions on Russian officials and others responsible for continuing the war on Ukraine.

The bill advanced through the House Rules Committee on Monday night, setting up a House-wide procedural hurdle called a "rule vote" on Tuesday afternoon.

If passed, the full House will vote on the sanctions bill on Wednesday afternoon, according to a preliminary legislative schedule obtained by Fox News Digital.

And with an increasingly vocal isolationist wing permeating the House GOP Conference, at least some Democrats will be needed to help the bill pass.

The package, pushed by Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and Graham, was in purgatory for nearly two years as the lawmakers and administration went back and forth to find a compromise that Trump and Congress could stomach.

Blumenthal defended the tariff language in the bill to Fox News Digital, "If Donald Trump wants to break this law, he will be restrained by the courts, just as when he broke the law on tariffs previously."

And Senate Democrats largely voted in favor of giving Trump limited tariff authority in exchange for the bone-crushing sanctions against Russia, despite raging against duties for years.

Though some raised concerns, like Sens. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., most Democratic caucus members gave a thumbs-up to the tariff power.

EXCLUSIVE: PENCE PUSHES TO RENAME BILL FOR LINDSEY GRAHAM, RECALLS FINAL TALK: 'BRING PUTIN TO THE TABLE'

That all came after Sen. Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., received guarantees from U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer that the tariffs baked into the sanctions package would just be limited to the top five energy trading partners with the Kremlin.

item.title: Supreme Court rejects Trump bid to revive strict mail-ballot rules before midterms
item.description: A lower court's nationwide block on U.S. Postal Service mail-in ballot rules remains after the Supreme Court ruled against the Trump administration.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court on Monday rejected the Trump administration’s bid to enforce new U.S. Postal Service rules for mail-in ballots ahead of the 2026 midterms, leaving a lower court’s nationwide block in place.

Justice Samuel Alito, joined by Justice Clarence Thomas, dissented, while Justice Brett Kavanaugh agreed the rules could not be implemented so close to the election.

item.title: Robert Kraft, Gillette Stadium boot Macklemore from Ed Sheeran tour over ‘Free Palestine’ rant
item.description: Macklemore was removed from Ed Sheeran's U.S. stadium tour after Robert Kraft's Gillette Stadium barred him over antisemitism allegations, grandstanding
item.content:encoded:
Macklemore is learning the hard way that concertgoers paying top dollar for stadium shows do not want a lecture on Middle Eastern geopolitics from the guy who wrote "Thrift Shop."

Macklemore was kicked off Ed Sheeran’s U.S. stadium tour after multiple venues refused to host him following his pro-Palestinian speeches and performances at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. The fallout escalated when New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft barred him from performing at Gillette Stadium, where Sheeran is scheduled to play Sept. 25 and 26.

The rapper opened Sheeran’s shows at MetLife on Sept. 4 and 5. Macklemore wore a keffiyeh, showed footage of destruction in Gaza, performed "Hind’s Hall" and led the crowd in "Free Palestine" chants. The song includes lyrics accusing Israel of genocide.

PINK HITS BACK AMID BACKLASH FOR CRITICIZING MACKLEMORE'S PRO-PALESTINIAN CONCERT REMARKS

Macklemore said the tour gave him a massive platform to promote his political message. He also claimed Sheeran told him Robert Kraft had rallied other stadium owners against keeping him on the tour.

Kraft, whose Kraft Group owns Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, cited the rapper’s stage behavior and what he called a "broader history of anti-Semitic rhetoric and imagery."

"Gillette Stadium has a longstanding commitment to providing a welcoming environment for all guests and ensuring that events held at our venue do not provide a platform for hate speech," Kraft shared in a statement made to ESPN.

"Based on Macklemore's recent actions, material shared from the stage during Ed Sheeran's shows in New Jersey, and a broader history of anti-Semitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community, we determined that his participation in the September 25th and 26th shows would not be permitted."

Tour promoter Messina Touring Group confirmed Macklemore’s removal from all remaining U.S. dates after multiple venue operators refused to allow him on the lineup. Eight of the remaining 10 tour stops were scheduled for NFL stadiums.

Macklemore’s controversial history includes a May 2014 performance in Seattle, where he took the stage wearing a bushy black beard, a dark wig and a large prosthetic nose. Civil rights groups, including the Anti-Defamation League, condemned the outfit as resembling historical anti-Jewish caricatures. Macklemore claimed at the time that the costume was a random coincidence.

BILL MAHER RIPS MACKLEMORE'S GAZA STANCE, SAYS CELEBRITY 'MORAL CONFUSION' IS FUELING ANTISEMITISM

That controversy resurfaced with the release of "Hind’s Hall," a song referencing student activists who occupied Columbia University’s Hamilton Hall. Critics argue that Macklemore routinely condemns Israel from the stage while ignoring the Oct. 7, 2023, terrorist attacks by Hamas that sparked the current war.

Kraft, who founded the Foundation to Combat Antisemitism in 2019, also addressed what he viewed as Macklemore’s selective presentation of the conflict.

"This decision is not about diminishing the suffering of innocent Palestinians or denying anyone the right to advocate on their behalf," Kraft stated. "But that advocacy should not come at the expense of the Jewish community or obscure the responsibility of Hamas, a designated terrorist organization whose horrific actions have caused immeasurable suffering."

Kraft added that supporting innocent civilians while standing firmly against Hamas and antisemitism should not be mutually exclusive.

"I would welcome the opportunity to sit down with Macklemore and discuss the facts, because ultimately our goal is the same: peace for all people, an end to suffering, and an end to all hate," Kraft said.

KACEY MUSGRAVES DIVIDES FANS WITH IMMIGRANT CHILDREN’S PLEA, FACES BOYCOTT CALLS TO ‘SHUT UP AND SING’

Macklemore responded in a social media post blaming venue operators and Kraft for his removal while acknowledging that Sheeran had been placed in a difficult position. He did not accept Kraft’s characterization of his comments as hate speech and insisted that losing his tour spot was a price he was willing to pay.

item.title: White House denies Trump influenced by 'pardon brokers' after '60 Minutes' investigation
item.description: White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said President Donald Trump doesn't know alleged pardon brokers after a recent "60 Minutes" report aired on Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
A White House spokesperson denied the suggestion that President Donald Trump's administration could be influenced by "pardon brokers" an issue examined by CBS' "60 Minutes" on Sunday.

During the show's season premiere, the long-running news program ran a segment on lobbyists reportedly negotiating for presidential pardons for particular clients based on alleged connections to the president.

"Presidents have been pardoning criminals since George Washington," correspondent Lesley Stahl said. "It's a constitutional power. No explanation needed. The Department of Justice does screen applicants and typically only recommends those who remorsefully seek mercy. But that's not always been the process. President Ford pardoned Richard Nixon. President Clinton, Marc Rich after donations. President Biden, his son Hunter, and Anthony Fauci."

BIDEN CLEMENCY BLITZ LEFT DOJ SCRAMBLING AS MANY COMMUTATIONS BYPASSED NORMAL VETTING, EMAILS SHOW

"President Trump, he's developed his own vetting system, pardoning political allies, including all of the January 6 rioters, as well as a string of unrepentant financial conmen who argued, just like him, that they were wrongly prosecuted," she continued. "How did these people get their grievances in the president's ear? Donations appear to help and those who can pay hire pardon brokers, lawyers and lobbyists who sell their ties to the president for exorbitant fees. It's a marketplace of money and mercy."

In a comment to Fox News Digital, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis denied that Trump was influenced by any "lobbyist" regarding his presidential pardons. She further criticized past presidential pardons by former President Joe Biden, pointing out that many of his pardons released violent criminals.

"Anyone spending money to lobby for pardons is foolishly wasting their money and the President doesn’t even know who these so-called ‘lobbyists’ are. The Trump Administration has a robust pardon review process which includes White House counsel, the Department of Justice, pardon czar Alice Johnson, and ultimately, the President himself as the final decider," Bis said. 

TRUMP GRANTS PARDONS TO 'PERSECUTED' MECHANICS IN RIGHT-TO-REPAIR CRACKDOWN: 'I AM SETTING THEM ALL FREE'

"The only pardons anyone should be critical of are from President Biden, who pardoned and commuted sentences of violent criminals including child killers and mass murderers, and extreme liberal Democrat Governors who pardoned illegal alien child rapists and attempted murderers in attempts to allow them to remain in our country," she added.

Fox News Digital reached out to CBS News for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

The latest season of "60 Minutes" came amid mass firings of longtime producers and correspondents as the network's editor-in-chief, Bari Weiss, attempted to reorganize the program. One former producer and managing editor, Guy Campanile, suggested in a private Facebook post last week that the firings were because they refused to compromise with "White House talking points."

‘PRIVILEGED’ HUNTER BIDEN, SPARED BY DAD’S PARDON, BLASTS TRUMP’S CLEMENCY POWER

"We would not compromise our principles or reputations by jamming unverifiable notions or White House talking points into our reporting," Campanile wrote. "We objected when told to conduct interviews arranged by the administration. We insisted on asking the most challenging questions to business and political leaders without fear or favor."

item.title: Mamdani blasts feds for waging 'campaign of violence and terror' against NYC's immigrants
item.description: Zohran Mamdani condemned ICE raids and federal immigration policies as New York City joined other sanctuary jurisdictions in a lawsuit.
item.content:encoded:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Monday blasted the federal government for waging a "campaign of violence and terror" against the immigrant communities he described as the backbone of the city.

He made the statements during an announcement that he and five other sanctuary jurisdictions are suing the Trump administration over a new rule expanding how immigration officials determine whether applicants are likely to become a public charge.

"The federal government has waged a campaign of violence and terror," Mamdani said.

"ICE has broken into our neighbors' homes, work sites and schools. And it has targeted those who have come to our country in search of refuge and in search of opportunity. These actions are an assault on our civic fabric, on our shared values. And no matter how much destruction they have already caused, it continues."

MAMDANI, LETITIA JAMES SUE TO BLOCK TRUMP ADMIN FROM REFUSING IMMIGRANTS OVER WELFARE STATUS

Mamdani further credited immigrants from around the world with helping build and sustain New York City, including by contributing to its infrastructure and public services.

"Immigrants from every country, from every continent, who speak every language and worship in every conceivable way, drive our buses and our trains, teach our children how to read, and tend to us when we are sick," Mamdani said.

"Immigrants fought for the 8-hour workday for fair pay and workplace protections that deliver dignity into the lives of so many," he added.

AMERICA NEEDS WORKERS, BUT TRUMP'S POLICIES ARE SHARPLY CUTTING LEGAL IMMIGRATION

The city will lead a coalition of five other sanctuary jurisdictions, including Chicago, San Francisco, Seattle, Santa Clara County and King County, in challenging the Trump administration’s stricter version of the public charge rule, which is set to take effect Friday.

The changes, issued in July by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), will expand officers’ discretion to weigh noncash benefits, such as Medicaid, SNAP and housing vouchers, when determining whether an immigrant is likely to become a public charge.

Under the previous guidelines, established in 2022 under the Biden administration, officers’ discretion was narrowed to consider only whether applicants were likely to become "primarily dependent" on government assistance based on cash benefits, such as Supplemental Security Income (SSI) and Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF).

According to the USCIS, the rule is intended to ensure that noncitizens are "self-reliant and not dependent on taxpayer-funded government benefits."

Mamdani described the changes as a "gross illegality" that will cause "irreparable damage."

"Make no mistake, this is an undisguised effort to strip New Yorkers of the services they rely on, the public benefits they are entitled to. Families, including those with children who are U.S. citizens, have already begun to forego essential services like SNAP, Medicaid, and affordable housing out of the fear that if they use these programs, immigration officers could use it as justification to deny them a future in our country," he said.

USCIS spokesperson Zach Kahler previously said the move is intended to safeguard the financial well-being of American taxpayers.

"The Trump administration is upholding the rule of law and protecting American taxpayers from subsidizing aliens who may become dependent on public benefits. USCIS is committed to safeguarding the safety, security, and financial well-being of Americans," Kahler said in a statement.

DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital.

item.title: House unanimously votes to eliminate 1-cent coin permanently
item.description: The Common Cents Act passed the House to officially end penny minting and establish cash rounding to the nearest nickel for cash transactions.
item.content:encoded:
Americans may soon no longer be able to offer a penny for their thoughts — because the 1-cent coin will be relegated to the ash heap of history.

The House of Representatives voted to send the smallest piece of U.S. currency the way of the dodo on Monday, passing the bipartisan Common Cents Act in a unanimous vote.

In addition to blocking the Treasury from minting any more pennies save for collector coins, the bill would also set up a framework for cash transactions to be rounded to the nearest 5 cents, in order to eliminate the need for pennies altogether.

AMERICANS SAY TIPPING PRACTICES 'HAVE BECOME RIDICULOUS' AS DIGITAL PROMPTS PUSH HIGHER GRATUITIES

An exception would be provided for cash wages, which must be rounded upwards if the total is not divisible by 5 cents.

Existing pennies will still remain legal tender.

TREASURY HAILS SUCCESS OF ANTI-FRAUD PROCESS THAT FLAGGED AND PREVENTED $99 MILLION IN PAYMENTS TO DEAD PEOPLE

The U.S. Mint stopped producing pennies in November 2025 after 232 years of circulation. But an act of Congress, if signed into law by President Donald Trump, would ensure a future administration does not reverse course.

The cost of minting pennies has risen dramatically in recent years, costing more than three times their value to produce as of 2025. The Treasury estimated an immediate annual savings of $56 million in a press release explaining the decision.

The bill was led by House GOP Conference Chair Lisa McClain, R-Mich., and Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee.

It builds on a past bill McClain led in the House that also passed the Senate directing the federal government to stop minting the penny, but that legislation did not include language on rounding out cash payments.

An additional provision would allow the U.S. Mint to produce nickels from cheaper material than they currently are made with.

Congress would also monitor any disruptions the new rule causes to Americans by directing the Treasury to examine its effect on low-income people, older consumers, debanked people, among other groups.

item.title: Common bedroom mistake could be quietly taking a toll on your health, experts say
item.description: A Tulane University study links sleeping with light on to higher risks of heart failure, atrial fibrillation, stroke and cardiovascular death.
item.content:encoded:
A new study from Tulane University is raising fresh concerns about sleeping with a light on, linking nighttime light exposure to a higher risk of cardiovascular disease.

Researchers found that exposure to more than 3 lux of light — roughly the brightness of moonlight — was associated with increased risks of heart failure, atrial fibrillation (irregular and often very rapid heart rhythm), heart attack, stroke and cardiovascular death.

Experts spoke with Fox News Digital about the potential risks associated with sleeping with a nightlight.

THE DAYTIME HABIT THAT COULD TRANSFORM YOUR SLEEP, ACCORDING TO NEW STUDY

Sleep is partially controlled by the circadian rhythm, the brain’s internal 24-hour clock that regulates sleep and wakefulness, according to sleep expert and neuroscientist Chelsie Rohrscheib, Ph.D., a sleep expert and neuroscientist based in Michigan.

"The circadian rhythm is strongly influenced by light entering the eyes – light exposure signals the brain to suppress melatonin production, a hormone that helps regulate the timing of sleep, while low light levels signal the brain to produce more melatonin," she told Fox News Digital.

DIETITIAN REVEALS SIMPLE EATING STRATEGY FOR BETTER SLEEP — AND ONE HABIT TO AVOID

"As melatonin levels rise in the evening, they help prepare the brain and body for sleep. Light pollution from various sources in our bedroom can trick the brain into producing less melatonin, which can negatively impact sleep quality."

Consistent light exposure will chronically reduce overall sleep quality, Rohrscheib warned.

"Sleep plays an essential role in many biological processes, including body and brain restoration, hormone release, immune system functioning, cognitive processes such as memory consolidation, brain waste clearance and metabolic regulation," she said.

FINDING THE SLEEP 'SWEET SPOT' COULD HELP YOU LIVE LONGER, STUDY SUGGESTS

"When sleep is consistently poor, these processes do not function optimally, which in turn elevates the risk for many chronic health conditions such as hypertension, cardiovascular disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, obesity, neurodegenerative diseases, certain cancers and mood disorders."

A 2022 Northwestern Medicine study found that just one night of sleeping with moderate light exposure (100 lux) disrupted glucose regulation while increasing heart rate and sympathetic nervous system activity, as reflected by reduced heart rate variability (HRV), Rohrscheib noted.

MORE NAPS, HIGHER RISK? RESEARCH LINKS DAYTIME SLEEP TO HEALTH WARNINGS IN AGING ADULTS

Sleep impairment is also linked to increased risk of mortality, according to Ashley Curtis, PhD, sleep researcher and assistant professor at the University of South Florida College of Nursing.

"Emerging evidence even suggests that it affects the gut microbiome, everything from digestion to immunity," she told Fox News Digital. "While the immediate evidence is strongest for disrupted sleep health, the downstream risks to your long-term health are substantial."

Certain groups may be more sensitive to nighttime light than others, experts agree.

"Shift workers, children, older adults and individuals with insomnia or mood disorders are especially vulnerable to the effects of light on sleep depth," Alex Dimitriu, M.D., a double board-certified sleep medicine doctor and founder of Menlo Park Psychiatry & Sleep Medicine, told Fox News Digital.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Curtis noted that older adults often become less sensitive to light, meaning bright or short-wavelength light has a weaker effect on suppressing melatonin than it does in younger adults.

"The caveat, however, is that older adults also experience a higher baseline prevalence of sleep disruption, which can bidirectionally impact the circadian system," she added.

There is also some evidence showing that bright light has a more pronounced impact on melatonin suppression in men, the expert noted.

For people with insomnia, who already experience chronic sleep disruption, bright light exposure before bedtime can make these underlying problems worse, as it further interferes with the biological circadian rhythm, Curtis warned.

Blue wavelength light from TVs and phones is the most disruptive because people’s retinas are most sensitive to it, and it maximally suppresses melatonin, according to Dimitriu.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"Dim, warm, red-toned night lights cause far less circadian impact – these are natural sunset colors one would see in the evenings," he told Fox News Digital.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Curtis agreed that warmer, dimmer light, which has a longer wavelength, doesn't have as much impact on melatonin production.

"Research shows that even if dim light impacts melatonin initially, it allows time for the body to recover," she said. "Therefore, it doesn't disrupt your sleep to the degree that brighter light does."

"While blackout curtains are recommended for optimal sleep, you don't need to have absolute darkness to maintain a healthy sleep environment," Curtis said.

item.title: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed says leaders must address ‘unpaid debts’ to Black communities
item.description: Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said that the country must confront what he described as "unpaid debts" owed to Black communities.
item.content:encoded:
Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said Saturday that the country must confront what he described as "unpaid debts" owed to Black communities, arguing that leaders have a responsibility to "understand" and "address" them.

El-Sayed — who is facing Republican nominee and former Rep. Mike Rogers in one of the nation's most closely watched Senate races — made the remarks while speaking at a meeting with women faith leaders hosted by the Woman Difference Collaborative in Detroit, according to a video shared by C-SPAN.

"When it comes to black communities in Michigan — when it comes to black communities in America — there are unpaid debts that have long since come due that we are unwilling to acknowledge, let alone pay down," El-Sayed said.  "And I understand that we need leaders who are going to understand those debts and address them."

ABDUL EL-SAYED PROTESTED AGAINST 'EX-TERRORISTS' WHO CONVERTED TO CHRISTIANITY, UNEARTHED REPORT REVEALS

El-Sayed made the remarks while responding to a question about how he plans to energize Democratic voters who did not support him in the primary.

He said his approach is to keep showing up, engaging with voters and emphasizing his record.

"But the question for me is, within my power have I done my best?" El-Sayed said. "And I will challenge people to look at my history and say, ‘Yeah, that man hasn’t done everything he could around the problems he says he cares about.'"

ABDUL EL-SAYED DISMISSES QUESTIONS ABOUT HASAN PIKER TIES ON 'FACE THE NATION,' PIVOTS TO GROCERIES

During his response, El-Sayed highlighted his work on infant and maternal mortality, asthma and lead exposure. 

He also called for expanding access to capital for small businesses and increasing investment in housing and schools.

El-Sayed, a former Wayne County health director, unsuccessfully ran for Michigan governor in 2018 before launching his Senate campaign. 

EL-SAYED’S LIBERAL AGENDA CLASHES WITH MUSLIM VOTERS WHO BACK HIM ANYWAY: ‘MALE VERSION’ OF ILHAN OMAR

The Detroit event also featured discussion of El-Sayed's public health record, U.S. aid to Israel, his endorsement of former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election, campaign attack ads from Rogers and criminal justice issues, according to C-SPAN.

El-Sayed's campaign could not immediately be reached by Fox News Digital for comment.

item.title: Gavin Newsom says he won't run for president in 2028 if Kamala Harris runs
item.description: Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom told CNN's Jake Tapper he won't run for president if Kamala Harris enters the 2028 race, citing crossover.
item.content:encoded:
Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom said he won't run for president if former Vice President Kamala Harris throws her hat in the ring.

"I don't know if she runs, but we'll see," Newsom told CNN's Jake Tapper in an interview released Monday. "But I wouldn't run if she ran."

"If she runs, you will not," a surprised Tapper reacted.

"Of course not. Why would I?" Newsom responded. "I wouldn't do that to her ... I wouldn't do that to you. I wouldn't waste everyone's time. Who needs that?"

HARRIS STOPS IN KEY PRESIDENTIAL PRIMARY STATE AFTER LEAVING DOOR WIDE OPEN TO 2028 RUN

Tapper, who was fly-fishing with Newsom in Montana during the exchange, appeared confused by the governor's stance. Newsom suggested spectators would feast on the "mutual-assured destruction" among Democrats competing for the nomination.

"I mean, you do whatever you want. I don't care," Tapper told Newsom. "But counterargument would be, like, you know, she had her shot. And you've never run, and she's run twice."

"Yeah," Newsom responded. "I mean, that'd be the approach to the campaign, certainly. That'd be the case you'd make. Pretty good one, actually. That's objectively true."

NEWSOM'S ATTACK DOG TAUNTS BUTTIGIEG OVER SOUTH CAROLINA VISIT AS 2028 FIGHT HEATS UP

HARRIS REACHES OUT TO SOCIALIST MAYOR MAMDANI IN LATEST SIGN SHE'S SHORING UP SUPPORT FOR POSSIBLE 2028 BID

"But I know what that means. I know her base of supporters. I know her friends. The Venn diagram on that is just pure crossover. I wouldn't do that," he added.

Newsom's name has long been discussed as a potential 2028 contender. However, the fellow Californian and 2024 Democratic nominee Kamala Harris may have the inside track to remain on the top of the ticket.

Harris holds a double-digit lead over Newsom among Democratic hopefuls by a 24.5-13.5% margin, according to the RealClearPolitics average of polls. Nipping at Newsom's heels within a five-point margin are former Biden Transportation Sec. Pete Buttigieg, New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff.

However, Ocasio-Cortez currently leads the Polymarket betting odds with over 19%, with Ossoff in second place with 16% while Newsom trails with 12.7% and Harris falls even further behind with just 8% odds.

item.title: Kaepernick tells 'The View' that NFL owners kept him out over politics and power, claims they donate to Trump
item.description: Former 49ers player Colin Kaepernick claimed the NFL donated millions to President Donald Trump and his administration, detailing his kneeling protest fallout.
item.content:encoded:
Former NFL star Colin Kaepernick called out the Trump administration during an interview with "The View" on Monday, saying the NFL supported the administration politically.

"Colin, just six months after you started protesting, you say you were forced to opt out of your contract with the 49ers, and you were never picked by another team again," co-host Ana Navarro said. "You sued the NFL for collusion, claiming that team owners were intentionally keeping you out. They’ve denied this. And it ended in a confidential agreement, though. So now as you look back, what do you think was the reason that not a single team would give you a chance to play for them?"

Kaepernick pointed to politics and power. The former quarterback joined the co-hosts of the liberal talk show to discuss his new book, "The Perilous Fight," in which he details his football career and the decision to kneel during the national anthem.

COLIN KAEPERNICK IS RIGHT ABOUT THE NFL'S 'PERFORMATIVE' RACISM CAMPAIGN — BUT HE'S ALSO A HYPOCRITE

"I think it was political," Kaepernick said. "I also think it was power. I think the reality is, one, I think it’s in important context: I didn’t protest the NFL. So their response to the protest is very informative in relation to where they stand politically. We’ve seen them donate millions of dollars to [President Donald] Trump and this administration."

Co-host Sunny Hostin agreed as the audience applauded.

"And I think the other part is the realization that the amount of support the protest had, there were also boycotts of the NFL because of their response. The NFL being approximately 70% Black also means that the players as the product on the field have power and control over where the league goes and where they head directionally," the former 49ers star continued.

Kaepernick said if NFL players unified around that and spent one weekend refusing to play, there would be no games.

"There’s no game, there’s no business and things would change very quickly," he said.

"You had a lot of people supporting you after that protest, but you also had a lot — getting a lot of hate, you were getting serious death threats from people who felt like you were disrespecting the flag, the country, members of the military," co-host Alyssa Farah Griffin said. "Were you surprised about the level of backlash that you received?"

"Yes and no," Kaepernick responded.

SUNNY HOSTIN BACKS NAACP CALL FOR BLACK ATHLETES TO BOYCOTT PUBLIC UNIVERSITIES OVER REDISTRICTING

"I think my years growing up were formative to give me some insight into what to expect on the other side of that," he said. "Also, historically, we’ve seen that, whether it’s Tommie Smith and John Carlos, whether it’s [Muhammad] Ali, we’ve seen it with Curt Flood, we’ve seen it with Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf. We've seen the response to Black people protesting, with Black athletes protesting."

"The part that candidly surprised me was the amount of pushback on a conversation of, 'Hey, police shouldn’t kill Black people.' That doesn’t feel like a controversial topic to me," Kaepernick said.

"I’m surprised at the level of pushback that people had on that, because we should all want to live in a society where everyone feels safe, everyone feels like they have the opportunity to thrive, and I think that was very revealing in relation to where a lot of people stand and the work that we have to do," he added.

Fox News Digital reached out to the NFL and the White House for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

COLIN KAEPERNICK TO RECEIVE MUHAMMAD ALI AWARD FOR FIGHTING 'RACIAL INJUSTICE'

2026 marked 10 years since Kaepernick began kneeling during the national anthem to protest police brutality and racial inequality in the United States. He has said that his activism was ultimately what ended his NFL career after no team picked him up once he opted out of his 49ers contract in March 2017.

In an interview earlier this month, Kaepernick said that the NFL was "actively blackballing" him and that he would no longer support the organization.

"I’m not gonna support an organization that one, is actively blackballing me, but two, has targeted my brothers who have been protesting as part of this as well," Kaepernick told NBC News. "I watch college football."

item.title: Ex-Dem insider exposes what Harris told top donors days before Biden dropped out: 'Insulting'
item.description: Lindy Li claims Kamala Harris secretly auditioned for wealthy Democratic donors while publicly insisting Joe Biden would stay in the 2024 race.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: Lindy Li, a former Democratic fundraiser who switched party affiliation over unheeded warning signs about President Joe Biden's decline in the 2024 election, believes Kamala Harris was setting herself up to poach Biden’s donors just days before he dropped out of the race — while still telling voters he could win.

Li said she threaded that political needle by staying far away from any criticism of Biden.

"It was all charade. She was auditioning for Biden's endorsement, and the way that she did it was by imposing a fake rule on her staff to not talk about her ascending to the nomination," Li said in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital.

Li’s chronicling of the months leading up to Biden's suspended campaign, which are included in her book, "Unburdened," adds more detail about how even those closest to Biden understood that his campaign would likely come to a grinding halt following his disastrous 2024 debate — and even before it.

EX-BIDEN STAFFER BLAMES BIDEN'S 'HUBRIS' FOR THE 'HELLSCAPE THAT WE LIVE IN': REPORT

As a top fundraiser for both Biden and Harris and someone who had achieved a high profile with the Democratic National Committee (DNC), Li worked with both teams to raise campaign contributions.

In the wake of the election, Li has gone public with much of her insider knowledge, raising the alarm over just how many figures inside the Democratic Party had seen the writing on the wall but remained silent. She also detailed how others, like Harris, quickly moved to prepare themselves for what would happen next.

In Li’s view, Harris prioritized face time with donors she knew could soon back her own bid.

"I was on the call; she would host calls with donors and pretend to support Biden and say there's no daylight between Biden and herself. All the while she was auditioning for those very donors," Li said.

HARRIS REACHES OUT TO SOCIALIST MAYOR MAMDANI IN LATEST SIGN SHE'S SHORING UP SUPPORT FOR POSSIBLE 2028 BID

Li recalled how, in one case, Harris addressed donors about Biden’s viability as a candidate two days before Biden bowed out.

"It was either on July 19th or July 20th. Actually, I think it was July 19, 2024; Kamala Harris held a call saying that there was no way that Biden would drop out and that she would stick with him until the end. And these were some of the biggest donors in the party," Li recalled.

Biden announced that he would no longer pursue reelection on July 21.

After Biden’s announcement, Li recalled that Harris moved aggressively within the Democratic camp to shore up support, insinuating that she had some form of Biden’s backing.

"She was flattering people left and right. The first 24 hours were a very intensive charm offensive on her part. And that's how she was able to consolidate it so quickly. She flattered people up the wazoo. It made it abundantly clear that Biden had endorsed her. And Biden initially — I don't know if people know this, but he didn't want to endorse her right away. It took him a while."

Notably, although Biden would endorse Harris later that same day, he announced he would not pursue reelection, his support of Harris came as a second message, roughly 30 minutes later.

Despite the vice president’s efforts to maintain her support of Biden and back his viability, Li recalled that some of those same donors didn’t buy her story,

LIBERAL CNN ANCHOR LASHES OUT AT DEMOCRATS' DECEIT AFTER JILL BIDEN'S ADMISSION ABOUT JOE'S DEBATE SHOWING

"A lot of us have group chats. And the immediate reaction is what an effing waste of time. What a charade, how fake. Like these are like the wealthiest people in the country saying that. They were very aware they were being lied to, that Biden was clearly not okay and to be told that he was okay when he was clearly incapacitated," Li said.

"It was insulting."

Representatives for Harris did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital.

item.title: McConnell returns after months-long absence for crucial vote
item.description: Mitch McConnell returns to the Senate floor after months of recovery from a fall, citing physical therapy and lingering effects of childhood polio.
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., will return to the Senate to cast his first vote following months of speculation on his condition and when the longtime lawmaker would reemerge into the public eye. 

McConnell said in a statement on Monday, the first day back for the Senate taking over a month-long break, that he would "cast my first Senate vote since I took a bad fall back in June."

"I’m really looking forward to being back on the Senate floor and seeing my colleagues. My recovery has been a long and often frustrating process, and the lingering effects of childhood polio haven’t made it any easier," McConnell said. "I’m still not quite back to 100%, but I’ve assured Leader Thune that, as I continue with physical therapy on the advice of my doctors, I will do my best to be present for tough votes when our Conference needs me." 

MCCONNELL IS OUT OF REHAB, BUT HIS ABSENCE HAS STUNTED A KEY REPUBLICAN PRIORITY

"Elaine and I are very grateful for all the continued well wishes from our fellow Kentuckians, and I’m glad to get back to more of business as usual on their behalf this month," he continued.

Having McConnell back changes the math for upcoming votes and future action on a possible budget reconciliation package to ram through chunks of the SAVE America Act and defense funding. He chairs both the Senate Rules Committee and Senate Defense Appropriations Committee, two key panels that could have a major impact on whether Republicans can move forward with the process. 

But first, he had to cast his first vote. 

His first appearance on the Senate floor since June was to vote in favor of one of President Donald Trump's judicial picks, Matthew R. Byrne, to be the U.S. District Judge for the Southern District of Ohio. 

MCCONNELL OUT OF HOSPITAL, STILL NOT 'MEDICALLY CLEARED' TO RETURN TO SENATE 

McConnell, 84, has not been in the Senate for votes nor committee work since early June after being hospitalized from suffering a fall at his Washington, D.C., home. His absence was further prolonged when he developed pneumonia, and went through a stint a rehab to further recover from the fall.

And his return comes as Republicans are again gearing up to vote on massive farm aid and funding package this week. The last time Senate Republicans tried to advance the bill it failed without McConnell's key vote.

The Senate Agriculture Committee is slated to again vote on the bill on Wednesday, and the committee's chair, Sen. John Boozman, R-Ark., teased that McConnell's return was imminent just before the announcement was made. 

MCCONNELL'S ABSENCE PUTS TRUMP AGENDA AT RISK AS KENTUCKY SUCCESSION QUESTIONS GROW

"I think they feel like he's moving in that direction," Boozman said. "So watch for him." 

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said that he had spoken with McConnell last week, and that the longtime Republican leader was "dialed in" on how campaigns for this midterm election cycle were going. Still, it's unclear how long he will stick around during the forthcoming three-week sprint before lawmakers make a jailbreak for the campaign trail in October.

item.title: Does the NFL's double digit ratings decline for opener show fan fatigue?
item.description: The New England Patriots-Seattle Seahawks opener drew 25.1 million viewers on NBC and Peacock, a 12% drop tied to the NFL's Wednesday gamble.
item.content:encoded:
The New England Patriots-Seattle Seahawks matchup last week was the NFL’s lowest-rated opening-night game since 2022, averaging 25.1 million viewers on NBC and Peacock.

That figure represents a 12% decline from last season’s Dallas Cowboys-Philadelphia Eagles opener, which drew 28.3 million viewers on the same network.

Considering recent changes to Nielsen’s measurement system, the broader multiyear decline and the double-digit year-over-year drop are notable.

The NFL and NBC will likely attribute the decline, at least in part, to the opener airing on a Wednesday for the first time. Moving the game from Thursday, traditionally a stronger night for viewership, to Wednesday was likely a factor — perhaps a significant one.

But that is more a consequence than an excuse.

NFL’S GROSSLY EXPANDED NATIONAL SCHEDULE IS MAKING REDZONE AND SUNDAY TICKET LESS ESSENTIAL

To understand why the NFL opened the season on a Wednesday, consider the league’s broader strategy.

The NFL views streaming and international games as its two biggest avenues for growth. But the Sports Broadcasting Act of 1961 prohibits televised NFL games on most Friday nights during the high school and college football seasons. As a result, the league could not schedule the Los Angeles Rams-San Francisco 49ers game in Australia on Friday, as it had the previous two seasons. Instead, the game was played on Thursday, pushing the Patriots-Seahawks opener on NBC to Wednesday.

The NFL will also play another Wednesday game on Netflix on the night before Thanksgiving. There will be four Friday games this season, including one on Black Friday and three on Christmas Day. Nine games will be played internationally.

On one hand, the expanded schedule means more football on television. On the other, it could lead to lower-quality football.

NFL SUNDAY TICKET IS NO LONGER WORTH THE PRICE | BOBBY BURACK

Fans saw last season how the additional windows, unusual days of the week, extensive travel, and limited rest hindered the quality of play. Teams playing on short rest, sometimes overseas, frequently looked sloppy and unprepared.

The changes also diminished the games’ sense of occasion. The Sunday slate, in particular, has become increasingly diluted by the addition of newly created national windows.

It should come as no surprise that fewer people watched last Wednesday’s opener than in previous years. Patriots-Seahawks was a sluggish snoozefest through three quarters. Working Americans faced two additional days of early wake-up calls that week. Another primetime game (Rams-49ers) followed the next night.

There is no reason to overstate the significance of the ratings decline. The game still averaged more than 25 million viewers. That is more than any NBA Finals game drew in June. The NFL is the most popular form of entertainment in the country.

Still, signs of fan fatigue and frustration are growing.

We have not even discussed how expensive it is to follow the NFL across its various television networks and streaming services this season. And it is expensive.

There is a reason the television networks did not cave and negotiate new rights deals with the league early, as some media analysts predicted.

Put plainly, there is more resistance to the NFL’s insatiable appetite for growth than the league may realize.

OutKick explained over the summer that raising the price of an inferior product is traditionally a poor strategy. The NFL appears to believe that standard does not apply to it.

Based on recent viewership trends, the league is slightly overconfident.

item.title: Obama, Biden judges draw fresh fire as Trump’s immigration court clashes heat up: ‘Almost impossible’
item.description: DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin says Biden-appointed judges are "almost impossible" to work with as immigration enforcement battles intensify.
item.content:encoded:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin is drawing a distinction between the federal judges he says the Trump administration can work with and those he says are "almost impossible" to deal with, singling out judges appointed by President Joe Biden as the administration continues to fight immigration battles in federal court.

"We find judges, for the most part, honestly, that we can work with in almost every area. But you've got some of the judges that were appointed underneath Obama and definitely, if they're appointed by Biden, they are almost impossible to work with," said Mullin on the sidelines of the RNC Midterm Convention on Thursday.

Mullin’s comments come as the Trump administration has repeatedly run into federal judges over its immigration policies, including recent rulings involving birthright citizenship and immigrant visa issuance. But while those court fights have received significant attention, Mullin offered a broader assessment of the judges he believes are most difficult for DHS to work with, specifically pointing to judges appointed by Biden — and, to a lesser extent, Obama.

WHITE HOUSE RIPS ‘ACTIVIST’ BIDEN JUDGE WHO UPENDED TRUMP BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP ORDER

In April, Biden-appointed Judge Brian Murphy blocked the Trump administration from ending temporary protected status for more than 5,000 Ethiopians, while in September, Biden-appointed Judge Deborah Boardman blocked enforcement of Trump’s August executive order limiting birthright citizenship, finding the order likely unconstitutional.

Mullin said immigration cases should be "cut and dry," arguing that they ultimately come down to whether an individual entered the country legally and has the proper paperwork.

He compared the issue to homeownership, asking whether someone has "the deed of the house you’re living in" and whether they legally own it.

Mullin also criticized state and local officials in blue states for limiting cooperation with ICE detainer requests, including in cases in which DHS alleges that detainees are violent criminals, drug dealers or known terrorists.

"It makes absolutely zero sense," Mullin said.

Beyond the court system, DHS is also facing battles with elected leaders in blue cities and states.

SPANBERGER'S ICE RESTRICTIONS DEALT MAJOR SETBACK AS JUDGE WARNS OTHER BLUE STATES

"Virginia is out of control right now. I mean, when you start looking at the great state of Virginia, who had a great governor in Governor Youngkin ... and now what they have, they canceled their 287(g) programs, they're not allowing any cooperation with ICE or any of DHS's law enforcement push to make sure we get the criminals off our streets," said Mullin.

Within weeks of taking office, Virginia Democratic Gov. Abigail Spanberger directed the state’s law-enforcement agencies to terminate their existing 287(g) agreements with ICE, which her administration said placed participating officers under federal supervision to conduct civil immigration enforcement.

Mullin claimed that 50% of recent deaths in Fairfax County were "at the hands of an illegal."

"I've said this multiple times, every death that happens at the hands of an illegal is 100% preventable. So why the governor of Virginia, why they wouldn't participate with us being DHS and forcing our nation's laws and getting their criminals off the streets make no sense," he said.

DHS BOSS REVEALS OVAL OFFICE PLAN TO 'WITHHOLD FUNDING' FROM SANCTUARY CITIES AFTER AGGRESSIVE NEW YORK BUST

Still, Mullin said the Trump administration would not force blue cities to accept federal assistance, arguing that DHS would remain ready to help communities that request it.

"What we’re not gonna do is force our way in. You’re gonna have to decide that," Mullin said, leaving the decision to individual communities.

In Danbury, Connecticut, the City Council amended its police hiring ordinance to allow lawful permanent residents and DACA recipients to apply to become police officers.

"I don't understand how you can be in law enforcement and yet you have no legal status. I just don't know what, in some of these very liberal towns and liberal states, what are they thinking," said Mullin.

"They're prioritizing criminals over law-abiding citizens. We are a nation of laws, and either we respect them or we don't," he added. "What separates us from a third world country is we don't believe in lawlessness and when you came in this country illegally, you chose to skip the line because we have a legal process."

item.title: Prince Harry's homecoming goes off the rails with brutal TV roast
item.description: "Saturday Night Live UK" skewered Prince Harry and Meghan Markle's return to the U.K., mocking their Netflix deal and royal family tensions.

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle were barely back on British soil before "Saturday Night Live UK" rolled out an unforgiving royal welcome.

KING CHARLES DRAWS ‘LINE IN THE SAND’ WITH PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE AFTER COUPLE CAUGHT OFF GUARD: EXPERT

item.title: Arizona mom used her flip-flop to fight off a coyote attacking her 4-year-old daughter
item.description: Brittany Cardinal was fighting off a coyote attack with a flip-flop when the animal bit her face while she shielded her 4-year-old daughter.
item.content:encoded:
An Arizona mom out in her neighborhood flying a kite with her 4-year-old daughter a couple of Sundays ago found herself in a fight with a coyote that refused to back down.

The coyote had started nipping at the little girl, according to mom Brittany Cardinal, and before she knew it, mom was swinging her flip-flop at it.

"We had gone outside because it was windy. And my daughter’s like, 'oh, let's fly a kite,'" Cardinal said, reports AZ Family.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

A normal activity on a windy Sunday afternoon. That was until mom heard her daughter scream and saw the coyote going after the girl.

"I picked her up and then I started yelling at it, thinking, of course, it’s going to go away, and then it didn't," Cardinal said. "So then I took off my flip-flop, and I was trying to scare it with that by like trying to hit it."

As the mom tried to fight off the coyote and get it to leave them alone, she fell. The coyote then bit her on the face.

ALASKA MOOSE HUNTER MIRACULOUSLY SURVIVES AMBUSH BROWN BEAR ATTACK, SAYS HE 'BLACKED OUT'

"I always hear people say like, 'you don’t feel the pain when like trauma like that happens,' and I mean, I really didn’t feel any pain," Cardinal said of the bite. "I just felt like the pressure of it."

Mom and daughter were eventually able to get away from the feisty coyote and make it back home. Mom had lacerations and puncture wounds on her face from the bite.

Arizona Game and Fish officials have removed several coyotes from the area following the incident and are testing them for rabies. They said that Cardinal did everything you're supposed to do during a coyote attack.

I guess everything except for getting bitten on the face. That I highly doubt is in the protocol. But everything else she did correctly.

Alex Flickinger, public affairs community liaison for Arizona Game and Fish, said, "You fight back, you yell at the animal, be loud with it, throw rocks, whatever you have to do to get that animal to just run off."

item.title: Vikings say Kyler Murray feeling 'pretty good,' participating in team meetings despite serious concussion
item.description: Kyler Murray entered concussion protocol after a vicious hit from Green Bay Packers defenders, but the Vikings head coach says he's feeling good.
item.content:encoded:
Kyler Murray’s start to his Minnesota Vikings career went awry on Sunday at U.S. Bank Stadium, as he was knocked out of the game with a concussion suffered on just the third offensive possession for the team.

The hits he took from two Green Bay Packers players were vicious, and after he officially entered concussion protocol, the question became whether he would be missing game time moving forward.

Head coach Kevin O’Connell, though, gave an update on his starting quarterback Monday following the Vikings’ come-from-behind victory to beat their NFC North rival, where he said Murray came into the building feeling "pretty good."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

O’Connell confirmed that Murray is in concussion protocol, but he said that the quarterback was participating in team meetings.

The Vikings will be taking it "a day at a time," he said, while the medical staff makes sure Murray passes each step of protocol.

In turn, Murray’s status for Week 2’s matchup against the Chicago Bears, who poured 59 points on the Carolina Panthers in their win on Sunday, is up in the air.

However, Vikings fans seeing the initial blow may have thought Murray would not be available next week. Instead, there is hope so long as he clears protocol.

Before suffering his injury, which came after Murray tucked and ran before a late slide led to the two defenders sandwiching him on the turf, he went 3-of-5 for 18 yards. He also threw an interception on the very first snap of his regular-season Vikings career, throwing a jump ball after the Packers brought a blitz immediately at the line of scrimmage.

Once Murray was off the field, veteran Carson Wentz, whom the Vikings kept on after serving in a backup role last season, was called upon to lead Minnesota for the remainder of the home opener.

The result was a composed, effective performance from Wentz, who completed 12 of 19 passes for 133 yards and three touchdowns in the 39-22 win.

item.title: Abdul El-Sayed dismisses questions about Hasan Piker ties on 'Face the Nation,' pivots to groceries
item.description: Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed deflected questions about Hasan Piker on "Face the Nation," pivoting to grocery prices.
item.content:encoded:
Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed rejected questions on Sunday regarding his relationship with Hasan Piker, saying that the race was not about "a Twitch streamer in California."

CBS News' Weijia Jiang asked El-Sayed on "Face the Nation" about Jewish Michiganders' concerns regarding his ties to Piker, the far-left streamer who has appeared with him on the campaign trail.

"There are Jewish voters in your state who are concerned about your relationship with Piker. You have condemned antisemitism but not called out his rhetoric directly. Why not?" Jiang asked.

JEWISH DEM DEFECTIONS THREATEN EL-SAYED IN MICHIGAN SENATE RACE DECIDED BY RAZOR-THIN MARGINS

Rather than answering the question, El-Sayed deflected, saying that voters were not asking him about Piker and that they were more focused on the issues impacting their daily lives.

"Weiija, with all due respect, this is the third time you’ve asked about a Twitch streamer in California. I’ve done four events in Michigan this week. You know what didn’t come up? Twitch streamers in California," El-Sayed responded. The candidate said that voters would rather discuss grocery prices, healthcare and the environment, among other things.

"I’m not interested in having a conversation about streamers in California because they are not raising the prices of gas and groceries," El-Sayed added.

El-Sayed is not the first Democrat to push back on questions about Piker. Last month, Rep. Debbie Dingell, D-Mich., demanded reporters stop asking her about Piker, saying that "Republicans are trying to make" the race about him.

EL-SAYED TORCHED ONLINE AFTER BRUSHING OFF QUESTIONS ABOUT HASAN PIKER CAMPAIGN TIES: ‘WHAT A PAL’

"I don’t agree with Hasan Piker on a lot of stuff, and I really don’t agree with him on some of the woman things he said. And I’m still trying to figure out, is it the reason he exercises and looks buff is why he has so many followers," Dingell said during a student town hall with El-Sayed and Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md.

Piker has been vocal about his support for El-Sayed, going so far as to call on Democrats to punish those within the party who oppose the Michigan candidate.

"You can't be out here saying like, 'Oh, I'm a centrist Democrat. And I think Abdul is a bridge too far.' That must be punished," Piker said during a stream in August.

While El-Sayed previously appeared with Piker on the campaign trail, he told Semafor in August that he had "no plans" to campaign with the controversial streamer. This came after Piker, who is known for his inflammatory rhetoric and anti-Israel stance, made a remark about Jewish Americans' support for Israel that drew the ire of several Democrats.

"People don't f--- with Israel any longer. And if Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they're singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone will come around and take action not against Israel, mind you, but against American Jews," Piker said during his stream on Aug. 20.

Rep. Hillary Scholten, D-Mich., condemned Piker in a statement, calling him "a hack who thrives on hate, shock and awe because he lacks substance."

ABDUL EL-SAYED PLAYS DOWN HASAN PIKER TIES AFTER STREAMER’S VIRAL ANTISEMITISM FIRESTORM

Several other Democratic lawmakers spoke out against Piker after he made the remarks, including Sens. Cory Booker, D-N.J.; Jon Ossoff, D-Ga.; Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich.; and Jacky Rosen, D-Nev.; House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y.; and Reps. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J.; Ritchie Torres, D-N.Y.; Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla.; Brad Schneider, D-Ill.; and Greg Stanton, D-Ariz.

El-Sayed also responded to Piker's comments, and while he did not condemn the streamer outright, he denounced antisemitism and rhetoric that puts the Jewish community in danger.

"I believe all Americans deserve the right to advocate for what they believe without fear of violence. This is particularly true for communities that have been intimidated for their beliefs in the past," El-Sayed wrote at the time.

"My commitment to Jewish safety is the same as my commitment to the safety of my own daughters," he added. "Antisemitism is a scourge, and we need to address it in all its forms. And I stand against any rhetoric that puts the community at risk."

item.title: Hochul accused of ‘hit job’ on behalf of teachers’ unions in act of ‘pure censorship’: labor group
item.description: New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul is accused of a free speech "hit job" after signing a law letting Letitia James fine groups contacting union members.
item.content:encoded:
New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul is being accused of conducting a "hit job" on free speech on behalf of teachers unions after she signed a law giving the state attorney general the power to fine groups deemed to be engaged in deceptive communications that falsely appear to be authorized by a union.

Hochul signed a law last week prohibiting people and organizations from using deceptive communications that falsely appear to be authorized by a union or union representative. The law, which took immediate effect, allows Democratic Attorney General Letitia James to investigate and sue to stop alleged violations, including those involving out-of-state groups. Courts can impose fines of up to $1,000 per incident.

In response, the Freedom Foundation, a conservative nonprofit that campaigns against public-sector unions, including teachers’ unions, says New York’s new law is a targeted effort to silence its outreach by making its communications vulnerable to government investigations, lawsuits and fines.

CEO Aaron Withe called the law a "hit job." He said the law "isn’t about protecting anyone," adding that it instead "exists because government unions in New York are terrified of an inconvenient fact: when public employees learn they don’t have to pay union dues, a lot of them stop. So instead of making their case to their own members, union bosses ran to their friends in the legislature and got them to write a law that makes speech illegal."

NATION’S LARGEST TEACHERS UNION UNDER FIRE AS CONTROVERSIAL AGENDA PUTS CENTURY-OLD FEDERAL CHARTER AT RISK

Fox News Digital reached out to Hochul's and James' offices for comment. Fox News Digital also reached out to the New York State United Teachers, United Federation of Teachers and the AFL-CIO for comment.

The law allows James to investigate alleged violations, issue subpoenas and ask a court to block communications deemed deceptive. Courts can impose fines of up to $1,000 per violation, including against organizations outside New York.

The New York State American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations (NYS AFL-CIO) praised Hochul’s decision to sign the bill, which she signed along with two other pieces of legislation related to labor rights. Mario Cilento, president of NYS AFL-CIO, remarked that the law will be "holding individuals accountable for fraudulently claiming to be union representatives."

He said the slate of bills signed by Hochul "put workers first."

In an X post, Hochul similarly framed the bills as prioritizing workers, writing, "Today marks a new day with even more protections, because I’ll never stop fighting for our workers."

"New York State gave birth to the labor movement. Over the last five years, I have continued that legacy by fiercely supporting the men and women of labor," wrote Hochul.

TRUMP UNLOADS ON AOC, MAMDANI FOR LAUGHING DURING SACRED 9/11 CEREMONY AT GROUND ZERO

Meanwhile, the Freedom Foundation has mailed and otherwise contacted New York public employees, including teachers, to inform them of their ability to leave their unions and stop paying dues. Nearly 7,500 New York public employees have used Freedom Foundation materials to cancel their union memberships, including more than 1,400 so far this year, according to the group.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Withe pointed to the 2018 Supreme Court decision in Janus v. AFSCME, which held that public-sector employees, including public school teachers, cannot be forced to pay union fees for collective bargaining or other speech because that speech can involve political issues protected by the First Amendment.

He said that while the New York law "lets Letitia James fine the Freedom Foundation for outreach the state decides 'impersonates' a union … all we're doing is telling public employees what already gives them: the right to leave their union and stop paying dues."

"This is an anti-speech law aimed at one kind of speaker," said Withe.

He asserted that the New York law was "copied" from a similar measure in Oregon, which the Freedom Foundation is already challenging in the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. He said his organization will "make the same case here."

Fox News Digital spoke with Ryan Walters, former superintendent of Oklahoma public schools and CEO of Freedom Foundation’s education arm, the Teacher Freedom Alliance. Walters called the New York law an example of "pure censorship and targeting of political opponents by Democrats protecting their union bosses."

INSIDE TEACHERS' UNION MAY DAY 'DRESS REHEARSAL' CRITICS WARN WILL 'GROOM' STUDENTS INTO DEM 'FOOT SOLDIERS'

"This is such a canary in the coal mine moment where if New York is allowed to do this - an openly socialist mayor, a governor operating as a tyrant doing the behests of the teachers’ unions - it's going to go on across the country, and our schools will not be able to improve in that kind of environment," he said, adding, "Where New York goes with this is going to be where the other blue states follow."
